Welcome to Closer Look, I'm Ed Linane. We're here in Washington at the Capitol Hill office of Congressman Tom McClintock, who represents California's fourth district. The congressman serves on the influential House Judiciary Committee, as well as the Natural Resources Committee. From that, he's also the Chairman of the Water and Power Subcommittee. He's married to Lori. Together, they've got two children. Congressman, thanks for letting us stop by
today. Well, thank you
very much. Used to be Chairman, now I'm the ranking member.

That's good enough. Congratulations on your recent re-election and now with your sixth term in office underway, you've got a full decade under your belt of being a member of Congress. Thinking you've probably got a few things figured out here by now, right?

I wish that were the case. What I have figured out is that we do have the finest form of government that's ever been devised as long as we recognize that and honor it. And that means the Constitution.

You know, I know there are times when there's a lot of talk about term limits, et cetera, but I would think somebody with some background and experience like yourself here in Congress, that would be a benefit to getting things done, would you think?

Well, what's most important, I think, is the fact that elected representatives are not the sovereigns of our country. The sovereign of our country is the American people. Everybody that they elect is hired help, and it's their responsibility to watch that hired help very carefully between elections and then to weigh in during those elections is where they keep them or throw them out and hire some new help.

You're no stranger to the political world before coming to Washington. You spent 22 years in the California State Assembly having served both in the assembly and the Senate. You also ran for governor during the state's recall election in terms of goals and vision and personality. What's changed if anything with Tom McClintock since you first ran for office back in the early 80s?

Well, again, I think over the years developed much deeper devotion to the institutions that resolve the differences that we have as a people. And we're in a period right now where we're seeing very, very intense differences. But we need to bear in mind that we do have the best institutions ever designed to resolve such differences as long as we're talking with each other as the American people rather than shouting at each other. And as the years have gone by, I've become more and more convinced of that.

You know, being a successful conservative Republican politician in California is a feat in itself, I think, especially in last year's election, which saw seven Republican seats switch over to Democrats. Obviously, representing the fourth district helps, but what else would you credit in helping you to accomplish multiple reelection wins?

Well, more than anything, I've been very consistent in my message over the years that I've served in public office, and that is that freedom works. The freedom that the American founders recognize comes not from government, but comes from what they call the laws of nature and of nature's God, of our Creator. We're born with those rights. They're not created by government. Rather, we create governments to protect those rights. And it's not just an ideological standpoint, as a practical matter, it has proven over the centuries to produce the happiest and most prosperous and most just societies in the experience of human civilization. I've found that the people of the Fourth Congressional District believe these things very deeply. And I think that's also true of the American people overall.

turn_text: The two things I hear the most often are the economy and the condition of the Sierra Nevada. My district pretty much is the Sierra Nevada of California. And as you know, we used to manage the forests to assure that we had vital, healthy forests. We removed excess timber before it could choke off the forest and burn. From that, we produced a steady stream of revenue and commerce for the region that supported our local communities, supported thriving economies throughout the Sierra. When we passed laws in the 1970s that made the management of our forests all but impossible, we've watched them do what an untended garden will do, and that is grow and grow until it chokes itself to death. And that's the condition of our forest today. That's why I've served on the Natural Resources Committee now for 11 years to try to restore the laws that allowed for the proper maintenance of our forests. And of course the economy, now we have that tremendous success there. The tax reductions and regulatory reforms that we've been able to win over the last couple of years are produced one of the most profound economic expansions in our nation's history. and we're seeing that across the country. Lowest unemployment rate in 50 years. Lowest unemployment rate for women since the 1950s. Lowest unemployment rate for Americans of African and Hispanic descent since they began keeping records. So we've had some significant successes there. We've had some successes in forest management. The legislation that I was able to get into the WIN Act is provided for expedited forest thinning in the Tahoe Basin, which has taken the bureaucratic delays from years down to months has shrunk the necessary environmental assessment from 800 pages down to less than 40, and is starting to show results there. turn_text: I know that you know that wildfires in California have grown to catastrophic levels. The cost for containment and rebuilding continually grows. When addressing this, you've often spoke about the need for improving land and forest management, right?

Well, exactly. And I was struck by something that Jerry Brown said after the campfire that wiped out the town of Paradise, killed 86 people. He said, well, this is the new abnormal. And I went back and did some looking at that and found out it's not the new abnormal at all. It's the old normal. In the last half of the 20th century, We lost about 250,000 acres a year in California to catastrophic fire. It was very steady, very consistent, about 250,000 acres. Last year, we lost one and a half million acres to catastrophic wildfire. something very bad has happened. But when we look at the destruction of paradise, we forget that was about 150,000 acres. In 1910, the big burn destroyed three million acres in Montana and Idaho, wiped out six towns and killed 87 people among a much sparser population than we have today. It was right around that time that we formed the US Forest Service. The Forest Service's job was to protect the forest, to manage them properly. And as I said, an untended forest is like an untended garden. If you leave it alone and don't tend to it, it's going to choke itself to death and ultimately will be consumed by catastrophic fire. And if you go back into the pre-Columbian days, you'll see that's exactly what happened. Prior to the discovery of California, the paleontologists tell us that in California, we would lose between 4.5 million and 12 million acres a year to catastrophic fire. That's what happens when the forests aren't properly managed. That's nature's way of dealing with it. Because of good management, we brought that from between four and a half and 12 million acres a year down to only a quarter million. When we abandoned those policies in the 1970s, we've watched the acreage being consumed by fire grow dramatically. We've seen an 80% decline in timber harvested off the federal lands over the past 30 years since those laws took effect 40 years now. And we've also watched a concomitant increase in acres destroyed by fire. There's an old maxim that excess timber comes out of a forest one way or another. It's either carried out or it burns out, but it will come out. When we carried it out, we had healthy forests. We also had a thriving local economy. And since we consigned our forests back to a policy of benign neglect, we've watched them consumed by fire.

turn_text: Well, here's one also connected to the long drought period that we just came through. Water shortages here in California, one of seven western states connected to the Colorado River Drought Contingency Plan, which recently passed in the house. You voted yes on that. What's the act do? Why is it helpful to people of California in the district?

Well, first let's just get a brief background of our water situation. Fortunately, we live in one of the most water-rich regions of the country in northern California. But, you know, everybody seems to think that the Colorado River is the great river in the West. Colorado River is a junior sister of the Sacramento. The Sacramento is a much, much larger river. The difference is we store 70 million acre feet of water on the Colorado. We only store 10 million acre feet on the Sacramento and lose most of the rest of that to the Pacific Ocean every year. What I learned, chairing the water committee for four years, is that droughts are nature's fault. They happen. But water shortages are our fault. Water shortages are a result of deliberate choice that we made to stop building dams. And the reason we stop building dams is because of the same environmental laws that have made the management of our forests impossible has also made the construction of new reservoirs cost prohibitive. We have not added a major reservoir over a million acre feet to our water system in California in the last, well, since 1979. Meanwhile, the population has nearly doubled. We're not going to solve our water shortages until we build more dams, and we're not going to build more dams until we overhaul the laws that have made their construction impossible. I'm just to give you one example. I've got the town of Forest Hill in my district. They get their water from a small reservoir called the Sugar Pine Reservoir, built years ago with an 18-foot spillway, but no spillway gate. didn't need the extra water at the time due now. That spillway gate is going to cost that little town about $5,000, $2 million. But that's not the price of the actual project. That's just the price of the gate. To the price of the actual gate, you then have to add another $1 million minimum in environmental studies, $2 million more in environmental mitigations, and $6 million is a forest service fee to move a trail that goes around the lake and about a dozen campsites. So a project that was viable for that little community to increase its water storage becomes a cost prohibitive boondoggle, and that's what stalling all of our projects. So, the act that you're referring to begins to move us back toward prioritizing water storage again, but we've got an awful long way to go. And we're not going to get there until we streamline and overhaul these laws that are making their construction so difficult.
